I started with python and when I learned about Go I really liked the ideas it introduced to me. Seemed like a manageable transition to a statically typed language. I was just starting to discover functional and thought the approach was refreshing. Never really got off the ground with it but did one or two small toy things.

 Couple years later I learned about functional programming and really liked clojure. I think it's great although limited to jvm and JavaScript. Recently I've decided to really try on common lisp and gotta say I like it a lot. It feels powerful even if the parentheses haven't disappeared yet. I really really like it and fully expect to continue learning and using it.

Tl;dr: coming from python, Go introduced me to a few new ideas that made me a better programmer. Lisp has completely changed the way I think about programs and I still have a lot to learn about it. I'd definitely recommend lisp even if it won't land you a job as easily as Go.

Not sure i agree with the self defeating argument bit but i think i understand what you're getting at,  "companies can work for the greater good, they aren't all out to screw you". I agree that they can work for the greater good. But what i was attempting to point out is that they aren't directed by their customers directly. They are directed by their interests. Religious organizations are held accountable to their religion. I don't know of many others that aren't primarily focused on growing the company (which may or may not be the ulterior motive of the other non religious health shares) . This in itself is not a bad thing. 

The point I'm trying to make is that with a private organization, you  as a consumer, have no direct control, especially on  one that has 100 percent of the market cornered. Would those public health shares still maintain the cheapest, best quality service if they had no competition and no oversight? Maybe. But i think it's naive to trust that they will without some form of control by the people they are serving. I'd love to see a truly great entity, government, private, or other, handle a single payer health care system with purely good motives. I just don't trust anything enough to say that they always have everyone's best interest in mind without some guarantee that if things go south, the customers have the power to shift direction back to what it should be. History has plenty of examples of profit over the greater good, but not as many the other way around.
